usage: air temperature takes 높다/낮다, never 크다
fixed phrase: 기온은 떨어지다/오르다, not 내려가다 in forecasts
일교차 means the daily high-low gap
영하 = below zero, 영상 = above zero
examples: When night comes the temperature drops a lot.
time clause + the set verb 떨어지다
일교차가 커서 아침저녁으로 기온이 많이 달라요.
The daily temperature range is big, so the temperature differs a lot morning and evening.
nuance: 기온 is the air temperature expressed as a number of degrees (氣溫, 기 'air/atmosphere' + 온 'warmth'), so it is the measurable reading the forecaster gives, whereas 날씨 is the whole overall feel of the weather (sunny, humid, windy) and 온도 is the neutral word for the temperature of any object or liquid like 물 온도 water temperature or 체온 body temperature. Use 기온 only for outdoor air. It pairs with 높다 high and 낮다 low, and with the motion verbs 오르다 rise and 떨어지다 fall; the big English-speaker trap is reaching for 크다/작다 (big/small) the way English lets you say a 'big' difference, but a temperature itself is 높다/낮다, and only the gap 일교차 or 차이 can be 크다.

mistakes: Saying 기온이 커요 to mean a high temperature; size words do not apply, say 기온이 높아요.
Using 온도 for the weather outside (온도가 높아요 about the sky); for outdoor air use 기온, and reserve 온도 for objects or water.
Saying 기온이 내려가요 by translating 'go down'; the idiomatic verb for the reading is 기온이 떨어지다.

usage: forecasts are watched/read with 보다, not 듣다 by default
맞다 = turn out correct; opposite 틀리다
quote source with 에서 + 고 하다
주간 weekly, 오늘/내일 일기예보 for the day
examples: I check the weather forecast every morning.
The forecast was right, so I grabbed an umbrella.
The forecast said it would snow tomorrow.
reported speech with 에서 ... 고 하다
nuance: 일기예보 is the official weather forecast you get from the news or an app (日氣豫報, literally 일기 'the day's air = weather' + 예보 'fore-report'), so it names the prediction itself, not the weather. Contrast it with plain 날씨, which is the actual weather happening now: you say 날씨가 좋아요 for today's nice weather but 일기예보가 좋아요 only when the predicted outlook is good. Koreans habitually 일기예보를 보다 (watch/read it) and judge it as 맞다 right or 틀리다 wrong, and they quote it with 일기예보에서 ~고 했어요. The English-speaker pitfall is treating it as a verb ('to forecast') — it is a noun, so attach a verb like 보다 or 확인하다, and use 에서 (the source particle) rather than 에 when reporting what it announced.

usage: set inchoative 시작되다 / opposite 끝나다, 물러가다
철 = season; 장마철에 = during the rainy season
전선 = the weather front that brings it
마른장마 = a dry spell with little rain
examples: The rainy season begins in summer.
During the rainy season laundry does not dry well.
철 period + a real everyday consequence
This year the rainy season is long, so I am worried about mold.
nuance: 장마 is Korea's long early-summer monsoon, the roughly three-to-four-week stretch around late June and July when a stationary rain front parks over the peninsula and brings steady, humid rain day after day. It is a whole climatic period, not a single rainfall, so it contrasts sharply with 비 (one instance of rain) and with 소나기 (a sudden short downpour): you can have 비 during 장마, but 장마 names the season. The word is treated as native Korean (it is not a hanja compound), and it lives in fixed phrases — 장마가 시작되다/끝나다 and the compound 장마철 'rainy-season time'. The pitfall for English speakers is calling any rainy day 장마; reserve it for the seasonal monsoon, and note that 장마 takes 시작되다/끝나다 rather than the falling verbs 오다/내리다 that plain rain uses.

usage: 태풍 moves, so it uses 오다/지나가다/북상하다
지나가다 = pass by, leaving calm after
영향권 = the affected zone forecasters mention
strength is 강하다/세다, named 태풍 + name
examples: Because the typhoon came, all the flights were canceled.
As the typhoon moves north it is gradually getting stronger.
nuance: 태풍 is a typhoon, the large tropical storm system that strikes Korea mainly in late summer and early autumn (颱風, literally 태 'typhoon' + 풍 'wind'). Even though the second character means wind, 태풍 is conceived as a moving body of weather, so it travels with 오다 come, 지나가다 pass, and the news verb 북상하다 move north — it does not 'blow.' That is the key contrast with plain 바람 wind, which 불다 blows: you must not say 태풍이 불어요. Distinguish it too from 폭풍 (a general violent storm, including at sea) and 돌풍 (a sudden gust); 태풍 specifically names the seasonal tropical cyclone, each one given an official name. Strength is described with 강하다/세다. The English-speaker pitfall is mapping 'the wind blows' onto 태풍 and producing 태풍이 불어요 — say instead 태풍이 와요 / 태풍이 지나가요.

usage: 뜨다 'rise' is the set verb, like 해/달이 뜨다
생기다 = come into being, a natural alternative to 뜨다
examples: A rainbow appeared after the rain.
time clause + the set verb 뜨다
A rainbow arched across the sky.
location 에 + a natural manner adverb
쌍무지개를 본 건 처음이라 사진을 찍었어요.
It was my first time seeing a double rainbow, so I took a photo.
nuance: 무지개 is a rainbow, the arc of color that forms when sunlight passes through droplets after rain. The grammar point that matters is its set verb: a rainbow 뜨다 (rises/appears), exactly like the sun 해가 뜨다 and the moon 달이 뜨다, because Korean treats things that emerge in the sky with 뜨다; you may also hear 무지개가 생기다 it forms. It is a pure native Korean word (no hanja), and it is firmly singular-in-feel — for a double one Koreans say 쌍무지개. The big English-speaker pitfall is borrowing the falling-weather verb and saying 무지개가 와요 (the way rain 비가 와요), or using English 'comes out' too literally; a rainbow does not fall or arrive, it 뜨다. When you simply look at it, it becomes the object: 무지개를 보다.

usage: 끼다 'settle in' is the set verb for fog/clouds
density is 짙다 thick / 옅다 thin, not 두껍다
걷히다/사라지다 = clears away; opposite of 끼다
앞이 안 보이다 = can't see ahead
examples: It got foggy in the morning.
past tense of the set verb 끼다 (꼈어요)
안개가 짙어서 앞이 잘 안 보여요.
The fog is so thick that I can't see well ahead.
Once the fog lifts, driving is much easier.
conditional 면 + 걷히다 in a real situation
nuance: 안개 is fog or mist — the cloud of tiny water droplets near the ground that cuts visibility. Its defining grammar is the verb 끼다, the same verb used for clouds 구름이 끼다, meaning the haze 'settles in,' so 안개가 끼다 is the standard way to say it gets foggy and 안개가 걷히다 that it lifts. Density is expressed with 짙다 thick and 옅다 thin — never the physical-thickness word 두껍다 — and a thick fog is 짙은 안개. 안개 is a native Korean noun (no hanja), and a close relative is 안개비 'misty drizzle.' The crucial pitfall for English speakers is the verb: do not say 안개가 와요 (treating fog like rain) and do not say 안개가 두꺼워요 by translating 'thick fog' literally; say 안개가 끼다 and 안개가 짙다.

usage: 가리다 = shield, e.g. with a hand or curtain
따갑다 = it stings on the skin
examples: Sunlight comes in well through the window.
The sunlight was so stinging that I used a parasol.
따갑다 on skin + real action 양산을 쓰다
nuance: 햇빛 is sunlight — literally 해 'sun' + 빛 'light,' the visible light streaming from the sun (the ㅅ in the middle is a 사이시옷, so it is written 햇빛 and sounds like '핻삗'). It is close to two cousins you should separate: 햇살 is the same sunlight pictured as soft, slanting rays and feels warmer and more literary (따스한 봄 햇살 'warm spring rays'), while 햇볕 is specifically the sun's warmth/heat you feel on your skin, the thing you sunbathe in (햇볕이 따갑다, 햇볕을 쬐다). So describe brightness/light with 햇빛, gentle poetic rays with 햇살, and felt heat with 햇볕. 햇빛 pairs with 강하다 strong, 들다/비치다 to shine in, and 가리다 to block. The English-speaker pitfall is using 햇빛 for the warmth you bask in — that role belongs to 햇볕 (햇볕을 쬐다 'soak up the sun'), not 햇빛.

usage: static location takes 에서 with action verbs
지다 = (shade) forms, e.g. 나무 그늘이 지다
그늘막 = a sunshade canopy in parks
examples: It was hot, so I rested in the shade.
reason + 에서 with the action 쉬다
The shade of the tree is cool.
Since the sun is strong, let's move into the shade.
cause 니까 + direction 로 in a real prompt
nuance: 그늘 is shade — the cool, dimmer area where an object blocks the sun, and it is the natural opposite of 햇빛/햇볕, prized as a refuge on a hot day (그늘이 시원하다 'the shade is cool'). The contrast every learner must nail is 그늘 vs 그림자: 그늘 is the shaded zone you can stand in and cool off, an area, whereas 그림자 is the dark shape an object casts — your silhouette on the ground (내 그림자가 길다 'my shadow is long'). So you rest 그늘에서 but you point at your 그림자. 그늘 is native Korean and also has a figurative sense of a hidden sad side (마음의 그늘 'a shadow over one's heart'). As a place, it takes location particles: 그늘에서 쉬다 to rest in it, 그늘로 가다 to head into it. The pitfall is using 그림자 for the cool spot ('let's sit in the shadow') — sitting place is 그늘, never 그림자.

usage: 타다 idiom: suffer in heat; opposite 추위를 타다
먹다 idiom = be struck down by heat
intensity 심하다 / 기승을 부리다 in news
examples: I am very sensitive to heat.
the idiom 더위를 타다 about one's constitution
Everyone is worn out from the heat that has gone on for days.
nuance: 더위 is heat as a felt, oppressive condition — the experience of hot weather rather than a number — formed from the adjective 덥다 'to be hot' plus the noun-making ㅟ, so it is the noun counterpart of 덥다 (mirroring 추위 from 춥다). Because it is a noun, it slots into idioms a learner must memorize: 더위를 타다 'to be the type who suffers in heat,' 더위를 먹다 'to be knocked down by heat (heatstroke),' and 더위가 심하다/기승을 부리다 for a fierce spell. Keep it distinct from 기온 (the temperature number) and from 폭염 (an officially declared heat wave): 더위 is the human feeling of it. The classic English-speaker pitfall is reaching for the adjective when a noun is needed — you cannot say 더위 to mean 'it is hot' (that is 더워요); 더위 is 'the heat' as a thing, e.g. 더위가 심해요 or 더위를 타요.

usage: 타다 idiom: suffer in cold; opposite 더위를 타다
강추위 = a bitter, dry cold snap
examples: 저는 추위를 많이 타서 손이 금방 시려요.
I feel the cold a lot, so my hands quickly go numb.
the idiom 추위를 타다 + a bodily result
며칠 지나면 추위가 좀 풀릴 거예요.
In a few days the cold will ease up a bit.
real forecast feel: 추위가 풀리다 + future
nuance: 추위 is the cold as a felt condition — the experience of cold weather — built from the adjective 춥다 'to be cold' plus the noun-forming ㅟ, making it the exact mirror of 더위 (from 덥다). As a noun it powers idioms you should learn as chunks: 추위를 타다 'to be the type who feels cold keenly,' 추위가 풀리다 'the cold eases,' 추위가 닥치다 'a cold spell hits,' and the vivid 강추위 'a bitter dry cold.' Keep it apart from 기온 (the temperature number, 기온이 낮다) and from the adjective 춥다 itself. The number-one English-speaker pitfall, just as with 더위, is using the noun for the adjective: 'I'm cold' is 추워요, not 추위; 추위 means 'the cold' as a thing — 추위가 심해요, 추위를 타요. Also note 춥다 describes weather/air, so you do not normally say 춥다 about a cold object (that is 차갑다/차다).

structuredNuance.t: 추위 is the cold as a felt condition — the experience of cold weather. As a noun it powers idioms you should learn as chunks: 추위를 타다 'to be the type who feels cold keenly,' 추위가 풀리다 'the cold eases,' 추위가 닥치다 'a cold spell hits,' and the vivid 강추위 'a bitter dry cold.' mistakes: Using 추위 where the adjective is needed ('I'm 추위'); say 추워요 for 'I'm cold,' and keep 추위 for 'the cold' — 추위가 심해요.

usage: snow falls with 오다/내리다, same as 비/눈
내리다 is a touch more written/poetic
to wait for the first snow
the day the first snow falls
a romantic date in pop culture
examples: basic 이/가 + the falling verb 오다
Because the first snow fell, everyone looked out the window.
We promised to meet on the day the first snow falls.
cultural set scene: 첫눈 + a promise (약속)
nuance: 첫눈 is the first snowfall of the season (첫 'first' + 눈 'snow'), and in Korea it is wrapped in romantic feeling: there is a widespread sentiment that meeting or confessing love on the day of 첫눈 brings good luck, so the word carries warmth a plain 눈 does not. Grammatically it behaves like the snow it is: it 오다 comes or 내리다 falls (내리다 sounding slightly more written), and you 첫눈을 기다리다 wait for it. Note the homonym trap: 첫눈 also means 'first sight' in the fixed phrase 첫눈에 반하다 'to fall in love at first glance,' where 눈 is the 'eye' — context tells the two apart. The contrast with plain 눈 is purely about that 'first of the season' specialness plus the emotional aura. The English-speaker pitfall is borrowing 'the first snow appeared/showed up'; like all snow it simply 오다/내리다 — say 첫눈이 왔어요.

usage: footwear takes 신다; remove with 벗다
-고 = and then go, the 'put on and...' chain
the classic material; 노란 장화 = yellow boots
비 오는 날 = rainy days call for them
examples: It rained, so I put on rain boots.
아이가 노란 장화를 신고 첨벙첨벙 뛰어요.
The child is splashing around in yellow rain boots.
장마철엔 장화 한 켤레쯤 있으면 편해요.
In the rainy season it's handy to have a pair of rain boots.
real advice + the counter 켤레 for pairs
nuance: 장화 is tall waterproof boots — rain boots or rubber wellies — worn to keep feet dry on wet days (長靴, literally 장 'long' + 화 'shoe/boot,' i.e. 'long boots' reaching up the calf). Because the hanja names height, 장화 implies the tall shaft, distinguishing it from ordinary low 신발/구두 shoes and from 부츠, the borrowed word for fashion boots: 장화 is specifically the practical, often rubber, rain-and-mud boot (고무장화). Like all footwear it takes the verb 신다 to put on and 벗다 to take off, and pairs by the 켤레 (a pair). The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 입다 'to wear' the way English uses one verb for all clothing — boots, like shoes and socks, demand 신다 (장화를 신다), never 입다; reserve 입다 for body garments like coats and shirts.
